x-m-m2-01.title: Making fractions wey get finite decimal even though denominator contain 3
x-m-m2-01.goal: Use counterexample show claim "if denominator get 3, decimal always infinite" no hold, and explain why these counterexamples happen.
x-m-m2-01.material: Jiho say, "Fraction wey denominator get 3 always turn to infinite decimal." How to read fractions: "9 over 12" mean 9/12 (numerator 9, denominator 12). Fractions below no reduce yet.
x-m-m2-01.thinking.1: Make examples wey meet condition yourself
x-m-m2-01.thinking.2: Work out condition where claim hold
x-m-m2-01.prereq.0: How to write fraction as decimal (division)
x-m-m2-01.prereq.1: Meaning of finite and infinite decimals
x-m-m2-01.prereq.2: Divisors and multiples of natural numbers
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose all fractions wey break Jiho claim (counterexamples). A counterexample na "fraction with 3 in denominator but still finite decimal."
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.hint.0: To find counterexample, you need "finite decimal even though denominator get 3." Wetin happen if you divide each fraction to write decimal?

x-m-m2-01.s.s1.explain: 9/12 = 3/4 = 0.75 and 15/30 = 1/2 = 0.5 get 3 in denominator at first, but after reducing the 3 disappear, so dem be finite decimals. 12/18 = 2/3 = 0.666…, 5/12 = 0.41666…, and 8/15 = 0.5333… still get 3 in denominator after reduction, so dem be infinite decimals.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.prompt: Now make counterexamples yourself. Denominator b must be multiple of 3 and at most 60, numerator a natural number at least 1 and below b. Make 3 fractions a/b wey finite decimals and all get different values. (Fractions wey get same value count once.)

x-m-m2-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Numerator must be natural number at least 1 and below denominator.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.ok.c2: Denominator na multiple of 3 and no more than 60.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Denominator must be multiple of 3 and no more than 60.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.ok.c3: Fraction turn out to be finite decimal.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.fail.c3: This fraction no be finite decimal (as decimal, e dey continue forever).
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.explain: Examples: 9/12 = 0.75, 15/30 = 0.5, 21/30 = 0.7, and 12/15 = 0.8 all get denominator multiple of 3 but still be finite decimals. 5/12 and 7/15 no fit reduce, so 3 remain in denominator and dem be infinite decimals.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one fraction you made and explain why e finite decimal even though denominator get 3.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write your fraction in simplest form and compare denominator with original denominator.

x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: You talk how denominator of simplified fraction gats look for finite decimal?
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.model.0: When we reduce 9/12, we get 3/4. The 3 for denominator reduce together with numerator 9; only 2×2 remain below, so e end exactly at 0.75.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.model.1: When we reduce 21/30 to simplest form, e become 7/10, and denominator 10 get only 2 and 5, so e become finite decimal 0.7. The 3 for original denominator reduce with 3 inside numerator 21.

x-m-m2-06.title: How many lines fit pass through one point?
x-m-m2-06.goal: Use relationship between slope and y-intercept of line through one point to make several lines satisfying conditions, and decide what information needed to fix one line.
x-m-m2-06.material: Point P(2, 5) on coordinate plane mean its x-coordinate na 2 and y-coordinate na 5. Make several lines y = ax + b wey pass through P, and think what extra information go fix one line. (Picture no dey; we go use equations only.)

x-m-m2-06.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one b first and fit a, then check all conditions (positive, natural number).
x-m-m2-06.s.s1.fail.c1: Slope a must be greater than 0.

x-m-m2-06.s.s1.fail.c3: If you put x=2, y no become 5, so e no pass through P.
x-m-m2-06.s.s1.explain: Put x=2, y=5 into y=ax+b give 2a+b=5. If b=1 then a=2; if b=2 then a=1.5; if b=3 then a=1; and if b=4 then a=0.5. If b=5 then a=0 and slope no dey positive. So only 4 lines fit meet conditions.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.prompt: We want fix exactly one line through P(2, 5). Choose all extra information wey, by itself, go fix one unique line.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.hint.0: Change each piece of information to equation or inequality in a and b.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one whether using am with 2a+b=5 fix both a and b to one value.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.o.a: Line too pass through point Q(4, 9)
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.r.a: This option check whether one extra point give one more equation between a and b.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.r.b: Compare with lines you make earlier to see whether "positive" condition fix one value or leave plenty.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.r.c: This option check whether knowing y-intercept fix a to one value through relationship between a and b.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.o.d: Line too pass through point R(2, 8)
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.r.d: You compare x-coordinate of R with x-coordinate of P? Think whether line through both points fit write as y=ax+b.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.r.e: This option check whether knowing slope fix b to one value in 2a+b=5.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.explain: Condition of passing through P na one equation, 2a+b=5, so one more equation needed. Using Q(4, 9) give 4a+b=9, and solving both give a=2, b=1. If y-intercept na 3, then b=3, so a=1. If slope na 2, then a=2, so b=1. Condition slope positive no fix values to one choice. R(2, 8) get same x-coordinate as P, so line through two points vertical and no fit write as y=ax+b.

x-m-m2-02.title: 0.999… less than 1?
x-m-m2-02.goal: Use two different kinds of evidence to rethink your first judgment about relation between repeating decimal 0.999… and 1.
x-m-m2-02.material: 0.999… na number wey get 9s forever after decimal point (repeating decimal 0.9̇, dem read am "zero point nine recurring"). Look at evidence one by one and see how your thinking about relation between this number and 1 change.
x-m-m2-02.thinking.0: Change your judgment according to evidence
x-m-m2-02.prereq.0: Meaning and notation of repeating decimals
x-m-m2-02.prereq.1: Division to write fraction as decimal
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.prompt: At each step, one more evidence come out. Choose judgment you fit make from the evidence wey show so far.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.hint.0: First think which judgment you fit make "from only the evidence wey you see now."
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether your earlier choice clash with new evidence.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.info: We never calculate yet. As you add 9s one by one, like 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, e dey near 1. Number wey come from continuing forever na 0.999…
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: Right now, wetin be the most reasonable guess about relation between 0.999… and 1?
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Guess fit change when new evidence show. Make we test am with fraction wey we know already.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Small-small less than 1. No matter how many 9s you add, e no reach 1
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: 0.9, 0.99, and 0.999 all really less than 1. But we never test whether we fit treat "number wey continue forever" the same way.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You fit guess say dem equal from beginning. But your reason weak for now, so test am with next evidence.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: E greater than 1. Since the 9s continue without end, one day e go pass 1
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Think about say only decimal places dey grow. Whole number part still be 0.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: E no be number, so we no fit compare am
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: E feel strange because e no end, but endless decimal like 1/3=0.333… still be number.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Division show say 1/3=0.333…. And 3 times 1/3 na 1. If you multiply each digit of 0.333… by 3, you get 0.999…
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: How this evidence change your first guess?
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.after: This method depend on one case, 1/3. Make we see whether totally different method give same conclusion.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: I dey lean toward equal to 1, because 1/3×3=1
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You use as reason say two values got in different ways (1 and 0.999…) come from the same number.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Still less than 1. 0.333… na approximation of 1/3, so multiplying by 3 still fall small below 1
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This choice treat 0.333… as "approximation." If dividing 1/3 give 0.333…, think whether dem be different numbers or same number written different ways.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: I no sure yet. I wan check with another method too
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This careful approach no rely on only one evidence.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: 1/3 and 0.333… na different numbers, so we no fit use this evidence
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: 0.333… na wetin you get when you divide to find value of 1/3, so find reason why dem go be different numbers.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Let x=0.999…. Then 10x=9.999…. Subtract x from 10x: 9.999…−0.999…=9, so 9x=9 and x=1. (Because the 9s continue forever, the decimal parts of both numbers exactly same, so when you subtract, all decimal places become 0.)
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now we don see both methods, how you go change your first guess?
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Look back: na evidence, no be feeling, change your judgment?
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Still less than 1. No matter how many 9s you add, e no reach 1
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You apply fact say 0.9, 0.99, … less than 1 straight to "one number wey continue forever." Compare with value wey the two evidence dey show.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Equal. Two different methods give same result, so e reliable
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This choice change judgment because two separate evidence agree.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Equal. We gats see 0.999… as one number wey continue forever
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This choice change judgment by treating am as "one number wey already set," instead of a "process."
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Greater than 1. Subtracting x from 10x give 9, so x bigger
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Read again steps from 10x−x=9 to 9x=9, and check how we find x value.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.reflect: At first, feeling say "no matter how many you add, e still fall short of 1" strong. But e reasonable to change your judgment when one case (3 times 1/3) and another method (10x−x) point to same result. Check whether na "evidence" or "mood" change your mind.
